lead: Two almanac figures become a height for any minute, a secondary port's tide, and the hour to cross a bar, round a race or make a tidal gate.

qa.q: How do I find the height of tide at a given time from the tidal curve?
qa.a: Mark HW on the top scale and LW on the bottom one and join them; from the time go up to the curve, across to the line, and read the height: **LW + factor × range**.

blocks.p: On a standard port's **tidal curve**, enter the HW nearest your time in the box, so the time reads HW−4 or HW+2. Mark that HW on the top scale and the LW of the same half-tide on the bottom one, the LW before on the flood, after on the ebb, and join them. From the time go up to the curve, across to the line, and read the height: **LW + factor × range**.

Backwards, factor = (height needed − LW) ÷ range gives the time. Between the spring and neap curves go the fraction that today's range lies between the mean ranges; beyond either, use the nearer curve, never extrapolate.

qa.q: How do I work out the time and height of high water at a secondary port?
qa.a: Apply the **secondary port**'s differences to the standard port: interpolate the time difference between its two tabled HW times and the height difference between MHWS and MHWN, then work on the standard port's curve.

blocks.p: A **secondary port** has differences on a standard port: time differences at two times of the standard port's HW, height differences at MHWS and MHWN, MLWN and MLWS. Interpolate each by today's value, then work the hour on the **standard port's curve** with the secondary port's times and heights.

From Swanage to Selsey high water is a long stand or a **double high water**, so these ports have curves drawn in hours **from low water**; pick the curve by the range at Portsmouth. Left of LW is the ebb, right of it the flood. Southampton holds near the top for two hours after the first HW; its five-hour fall runs harder than the seven-hour rise.

sections.title: Under the keel, over the mast

qa.q: How do I calculate the depth under my keel in a swell?
qa.a: Charted depth + height of tide, minus draught, **half the swell** for the troughs and squat at speed: 5.4 + 1.2 − 1.0 − 0.3 − 2.2 leaves 3.1 m under the keel.

blocks.p: Depth = charted depth + height of tide; take off draught, **half the swell** for the troughs, and squat at speed. At anchor, depth now − the fall to come must cover draught and margin, and springs make tomorrow's LW lower. Least charted depth = draught + margin − height of LW. A sill gauge already reads the depth over the sill.
Overhead: room = charted clearance + HAT − height of tide. A power cable's **safe clearance** allows for arcing; never trim it by eye.

A forecast **storm surge** adds to the prediction and already holds the pressure effect: never twice. A positive surge bites on a spring HW; a negative one takes water off a shallow passage. North Sea: a deep low tracking SE, a northerly gale behind it.

qa.q: When is it safe to cross a bar at a river or harbour entrance?
qa.a: On the flood and in daylight: a **bar** breaks when the depth falls to about 1.3 times the swell height, sooner in a long swell, and is worst on the ebb against the swell.

blocks.p: To float over drying ground you need **drying height + draught + margin** of tide; she touches when the tide falls to drying height + draught. Arrive just before HW and let her settle, after sounding the berth: level, firm, clear. Heel a fin keel slightly to the wall, rig a fender board, and tend the lines all night. Go on while the tides are making; once they **take off**, the next HW may not float you.

A **bar** breaks when the depth falls to about 1.3 times the swell height, sooner in a long swell, worst on the ebb against the swell. Cross on the flood, in daylight; otherwise stand off or go to a harbour without one. Bars shift: trust the latest notice, and a closed bar is closed.

sections.title: How hard, and when

qa.q: What do the numbers 18,34 on a tidal stream atlas arrow mean?
qa.a: 1.8 knots at mean neaps and 3.4 knots at mean springs; interpolate between them by today's range at the atlas's **own reference port**. With today's range halfway between the mean ranges, the rate is 2.6 kn.

refs: Tidal streams — slow and fast boats

blocks.p: An atlas arrow marked 18,34 means 1.8 kn at mean neaps, 3.4 kn at mean springs. Interpolate by today's range at the atlas's **own reference port**; this line you may extend beyond springs and neaps. French tables grade a tide by its **coefficient**: 45 mean neaps, 95 mean springs. Near an amphidromic point the range is small but the stream strong: rates come from the atlas.

blocks.p: Set = rate × time in the stream, so a slow yacht is set further. At 20 knots the stream hardly changes the time; wind against tide at each end decides.

If the stream turns, the slow one wins back
Fuel against a stream: hours × litres/hour

blocks.p: A **tidal gate** opens only with the stream. Time to leave = time it opens − distance ÷ speed over the ground. Take an unavoidable foul tide where it is weakest, the fair one through the narrows.

sections.title: Where the stream breaks the sea

qa.q: How do I round a headland with a tidal race safely?
qa.a: Outside the **race**'s charted extent plus a margin, wider at night and in fog, or through it at slack water. The inshore passage, a few cables off, is for settled weather, neaps and daylight.

blocks.p: A **race** forms where a strong stream sweeps past a headland and lies downstream, so it changes sides with the stream. **Overfalls** stand over an uneven bottom. Wind against stream steepens every sea: the water feels wind plus stream.

fig.note: The race lies downstream: here E and SE of the point

blocks.p: The **inshore passage**, a few cables off: settled weather, neaps, daylight, the pilot's time. Outside: the race's charted extent plus a margin, wider at night and in fog. Or through at slack: work back from the start of the fair stream, given as hours from HW at a reference port. Springs double the rate and shorten the slack; if the passage outlasts the slack, go at neaps, and a slow yacht arriving late waits a tide. Before a race: harnesses, hatches, briefing; planing boats slow down.

fig.note: A inshore passage · B the race · C outside, the default

qa.q: Do I need to allow for tidal streams in mid-ocean, off the continental shelf?
qa.a: Hardly: beyond the shelf the streams are weak and **rotary** and nearly cancel over a cycle. Plan with the routeing chart's mean current, check it by fixes, and apply a set that holds for half a day.

blocks.p: Beyond the shelf the streams are weak and **rotary** and nearly cancel over a cycle. Plan with the routeing chart's mean current, check it by fixes, and keep applying a set that holds for half a day. After a gale the **wind drift** sets right of downwind in the northern hemisphere. Off Portugal the Portugal Current runs south in summer with the northerlies; in winter a N-going current follows the shelf edge. In the Strait of Gibraltar the surface flows east into the Mediterranean, and the W-going streams run inshore.
